title: Continuous Delivery
summary: Faster is safer: small, frequent, flag-guarded releases on a predictable release train beat big launches — automated, data-driven, and isolated from the release itself.
text: Continuous Delivery's counterintuitive core claim: "faster is safer." Small, frequent batches mean fewer changes to troubleshoot per release, lower risk per release, and cheaper abandoned work — while a predictable release train forces down the per-release cost. The enabling levers are architectural (modularity), procedural (flag guarding, deadlines, staged rollouts), and cultural ("one release responsibility is to protect the product from the developers"). The big idea An organization's velocity is bottlenecked by time to deployment, and deployment isn't a one-time event: "no software is perfect at first launch, and the only guarantee is that you'll have to update it. Quickly." The value of code is realized when features reach users, not at submission, so shrinking the gap between "code complete" and user feedback minimizes the cost of work in progress — the same lesson Martin Fowler draws ("the biggest risk to any software effort is that you end up building something that isn't useful") and David Weekly captures: the launch never lands, it begins a learning cycle that is never complete. The chapter's six idioms all serve one tenet: over time, smaller batches of changes result in higher quality — faster is safer. The idioms: agility (release frequently, in small batches), automation (remove the repetitive overhead of frequent releases), isolation (modular architecture so changes are separable and troubleshooting is easy), reliability (measure health indicators like crashes and latency), data-driven decisions (A/B testing on health metrics), and phased rollout (a few users before everyone). Frequent releases feel risky, but that's backwards: so few changes separate consecutive releases that troubleshooting becomes trivial. And because the ideal isn't reachable immediately, the intermediate step is cultural — "teams can build their readiness to deploy at any time without actually doing so." Section by section 24.1 Idioms of Continuous Delivery at Google The core tenet — smaller batches yield higher quality — "can seem deeply controversial" to teams lacking the prerequisites (CI and testing), so Google focuses on aspects that deliver value independently en route to full CD. The idioms list (agility, automation, isolation, reliability, data-driven decisions, phased rollout) is a maturity checklist. In the limit, every change goes through the QA pipeline and deploys automatically; most teams aren't there, so culture change and gradually built confidence are part of the process. 24.2 Velocity Is a Team Sport: How to Break Up a Deployment into Manageable Pieces As a team grows or splits, an antipattern emerges: a subteam branches off its code to avoid stepping on anyone's feet, then struggles with integration and culprit finding. Google prefers developing at head in the shared codebase with CI testing, automatic rollbacks, and culprit finding (Chapter 23's machinery). The cautionary example is YouTube: a large monolithic Python application whose release process needed Build Cops, release managers, volunteers, multiple cherry-picks and respins, and a 50-hour manual regression-testing cycle by a remote QA team. High release cost creates a vicious cycle — wait to test a bit more, squeeze in "just one more feature" — until the process is laborious, slow, error prone, the release experts have burned out and left, and "nobody even knows how to troubleshoot those strange crashes," leaving everyone panicky at the thought of pushing the button. The instinctive fix — slow the cadence, extend stability periods — buys only short-term stability while strangling velocity. Resist the "obvious operational fixes" (traditional planning models, more governance and oversight, risk reviews, rewarding low-risk low-value features). The best-return investment is architectural: migrating to microservices, or rewriting from scratch to establish modularity. Either takes months and hurts in the short term, but the operational-cost and cognitive-simplicity gains pay off "over an application's lifespan of years." 24.3 Evaluating Changes in Isolation: Flag-Guarding Features The key to reliable continuous releases: engineers "flag guard" all changes. As a product grows, many features at various stages of development coexist in one binary; flags control the inclusion or expression of each feature, differently for development and release builds (build tools can even strip disabled features if the language permits). New code ships alongside the old codepath behind its flag: if it works, remove the old path and launch fully in a later release; if it breaks, flip the flag via a dynamic config update, decoupled from the binary release. Flag guards also decouple marketing from deployment. In the old world, press releases had to be timed with binary rollouts, and features went live before being announced, at real risk of early discovery. With a flag, the feature turns on immediately before the announcement. Caveats: flag-guarded code "is not a perfect safety net for truly sensitive features" (unobfuscated code can be scraped, and not every feature can be hidden without complexity), and even config changes must roll out carefully — turning a flag on for 100% of users at once is not a great idea, so a configuration service that manages safe config rollouts is a good investment. 24.4 Striving for Agility: Setting Up a Release Train Google's oldest binary, Search, is a codebase with code dating to at least 2003. Mobile features were shoehorned into a "hairball" written for servers; at one point releases hit production weekly at best, "often based on luck." When Sheri Shipe took on release velocity, each cycle took groups of engineers days (build, integrate data, test, manually triage every bug for quality/UX/revenue impact), so developers never knew when their feature would ship — and launches couldn't be scheduled. Over several years, a dedicated team automated what it could, set feature-submission deadlines, and simplified plug-in/data integration: a new Search binary every other day, consistently. Two trade-offs were baked in: No Binary Is Perfect. A build incorporating tens or hundreds of developers' work can't have every bug fixed; releases involve constant judgment calls (does moving a line two pixels affect ad revenue? does an altered shade hurt visually impaired users?). KPI metrics with clear thresholds let imperfect features launch (the SRE error-budget idea: perfection is rarely the right goal) and bring clarity to contentious decisions. The memorable story: a bug in a dialect spoken on one Philippine island returned a blank page instead of search answers. After running from office to office for data — and being deferred upward by every quality engineer — the team put it to Search's SVP: "no matter how small your island, you should get reliable and accurate search results" — the release was delayed and the bug fixed. Meet Your Release Deadline. "If you're late for the release train, it will leave without you" — "deadlines are certain, life is not." At some point you turn away developers, and no pleading gets a feature onto today's release. The rare exception is the Friday-evening cavalry: six engineers with an NBA-contract feature that must ship before tomorrow's game, and a bleary-eyed release engineer with a kid's birthday and balloons to pick up explaining it takes four hours to cut and test a binary. A regular train defuses this: miss one and you catch the next in hours, not days — limiting panic and preserving release engineers' work–life balance. 24.5 Quality and User-Focus: Ship Only What Gets Used Bloat is the "unfortunate side effect" of most life cycles, magnified by a fast release train. For client software the user's device pays in space, download, and data costs — even for features never used — while developers pay in slower builds, complex deployments, and rare bugs. title: Compute as a Service
summary: ‘Just give me hardware to run my stuff,’ made scalable: Borg-style scheduling, containers, one shared compute pool — and software written as cattle to benefit.
text: Compute as a Service (CaaS) turns "give me hardware to run my stuff" into an automated, multitenant system that survives organizational growth — Google's Borg being the precursor of Kubernetes and Mesos. The software side matters as much as the infrastructure: programs must be built as cattle (stateless, failure-tolerant, service-discovery-based) to reap the benefits. And the compute choice is a high-lock-in, abstraction-level trade-off — one shared pool maximizes efficiency, but customization pressures and serverless alternatives complicate it. The big idea After writing code you need hardware to run it on; renting and managing that hardware is CaaS. The chapter traces how the naive solution — SFTP the code onto a machine, SSH in, compile, run — becomes unmaintainable at scale, via Jeff Dean's 2002 complaint about running an automated data-processing task: getting a list of 50+ machines, starting a process on each, monitoring each by hand, with a human-implemented "sign-up" file to throttle usage and no automatic migration when a machine dies. Each pain point in that quote spawned a layer of automation: deployment, monitoring, healing, scheduling, and eventually bin-packing containers onto a shared fleet. The deeper lesson is that CaaS is a contract between two engineering organizations: the infrastructure team automates the environment, and application teams must write software that honors the model — replaceable replicas, transient local state, no hardcoded hostnames, idempotent request handling. When both sides hold up their end, the payoff is enormous: self-healing services, batch workloads soaking up otherwise-wasted serving slack ("we run batch effectively for free"), and a single abstraction layer that absorbs machine changes so thousands of application teams don't have to. Section by section 25.1 Taming the Compute Environment The evolution of Borg shows how each automation step answers the growth of the organization: Automation of toil. Simple automations come first: scripts to deploy binaries in parallel, exported monitoring metrics (the open-source equivalents being Grafana/Prometheus dashboards), agents that detect anomalies and kill unhealthy processes, and while true; do run && break; done loops — the cloud equivalent being an autohealing policy. The bigger step is automated scheduling: a central service knows the machine list and, on demand, picks unoccupied machines and deploys your binary — eliminating the hand-maintained sign-up file. Add machine-health scanning (e.g., mass disk read errors), automated first-line fixes (reboots, disk scans), and rescheduling work onto a new machine when one dies, and Jeff Dean's nightmare is fully automated. The result, the 2002 Global WorkQueue design document, was an early internal CaaS. Containerization and multitenancy. A one-to-one machine-to-program mapping wastes resources in several ways: job types outnumber machine types (provisioned for the largest), machines take months to arrive while programs grow (so machines are overprovisioned), and old heterogeneous machines linger. The fix: declare per-program resource requirements and let the scheduler bin-pack replicas. But neighbors interfere — CPU overruns cause latency blips, RAM overruns cause OOM kills or disk swap (Google universally prefers the OOM kill), dependency versions collide, /tmp gets fought over, and sensitive data needs protection. Hence isolation. VMs isolate well but carry a full OS's resource and boot-time overhead — wrong for batch jobs — so Borg's 2003 designers chose containers: cgroups (contributed to Linux in 2007) plus chroot jails, bind mounts, and union/overlay filesystems (Docker and LMCTFY are open-source descendants). Isolation failures are discovered over years: in 2011, Borg found the default 32,000-PID limit had become a real isolation boundary. Rightsizing and autoscaling. The 2006 Borg scheduled work from human-supplied configuration numbers — but those aren't numbers humans interact with daily, they go stale as programs grow, and stale slack ends in outages. Automating them proved "surprisingly tricky": only recently has more than half of Borg's fleet-wide resource usage been set by rightsizing automation (though that covers a larger fraction of configurations, freeing most engineers from sizing). This embodies "easy things should be easy, and complex things should be possible." Summary. Three growth axes — number of applications, number of copies, size of the largest application — demand ever more involved automation (GPU/TPU scheduling being a major recent Borg change). Even datacenter turnup, once a weeks-long manual specialty process, is becoming fully automated. 25.2 Writing Software for Managed Compute Managed compute "took profound changes to the way we write and think about software": Architecting for failure. Processing a million documents on one machine takes 12 days; across 200 machines, 100 minutes — but the Borg scheduler may unilaterally kill and move any worker (kernel updates, bad disks, bin-packing reshuffles; "as a software author, I should neither know nor care why"). The pets versus cattle metaphor (attributed to Bill Baker) captures the required posture: pets get nursed back to health by panicked humans, with maintenance burden growing linearly or worse; cattle — replica001 to replica100 — are stamped out automatically, enabling self-healing. Cattle alone isn't enough, though: static work assignment means every lost worker wastes up to 50 minutes. Instead, split the work into 1,000 chunks of 1,000 documents, with workers reporting results and picking up the next chunk dynamically — the MapReduce (later Flume) pattern. For serving jobs, Borg signals rescheduling intent ahead of time so a container can refuse new requests and finish in-flight ones, with load balancers honoring the refusal. Batch versus serving. Batch jobs (logs analysis, ML training) run to completion and care about throughput; serving jobs run indefinitely, care about per-request latency, and have longer startup times. Serving jobs are naturally failure-resistant (requests are inherently small dynamically-assigned chunks) — except leaders holding system state, statically sharded data (100 servers each holding 1%; lose one, lose that slice), and servers known by hostname. Managing state. Replacing a cattle job loses all in-process and local state, so local state is transient and "real storage" lives elsewhere. The simplest rule: anything that must survive a request or a chunk goes to durable external storage; if all local state is immutable, failure resistance is nearly free. Persistent state can still be managed by cattle through state replication (3–5 replicas, consensus for writes — hard enough that Google built GFS, Bigtable, and Spanner to enable it). Local transient storage has legitimate uses: caching (the key lesson: "provision the cache to meet your latency goals, but provision the core application for the total load," so losing the cache layer degrades latency instead of causing an outage), warm-up data loads, and batching writes when some loss is acceptable (monitoring data), with periodic checkpointing to split long computations. Connecting to a service. A hardcoded hostname means your replicas aren't cattle. The answer is a durable service identifier resolved by a service discovery system the scheduler writes to; clients resolve at startup, monitor in the background, and load balancing decouples them further. Consequences: requests must sometimes be retried (even server-to-database), APIs should handle this gracefully, and mutating requests need idempotency — the pizza-order pattern of client-assigned identifiers, where re-submitting an existing ID just reports success. Even split-brain happens: when a "lost" machine comes back, two replicas both believe they're replica072; the address-resolution system disambiguates, and idempotency absorbs the duplicate work.
